name: Conversation, Not Just Announcements
title: Conversation, Not Just Announcements
answer: This idea is two way translated messaging through TalkingPoints, so families can reply to teachers in their own language and get replies in theirs. It matters because it turns one way announcements into conversations where parents can ask questions, share concerns, and tell teachers what they know about their children. The book also warns that replies must be personal and that sensitive matters belong in a call with an interpreter.

sections.body: The idea is that family communication should be a conversation rather than a stream of announcements. Two way translated messaging through TalkingPoints lets parents reply to teachers in their own language and receive replies in theirs. That gives parents a way to ask questions, share concerns, and tell teachers what they know about their children. The problem it solves is the one way pattern in which schools send information out but families cannot easily respond in their own language. It also sets a standard for the reply, because a message that feels automated can damage trust more than silence would.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher uses two way translated messaging through TalkingPoints so parents can reply in their own language and receive replies in theirs. The teacher should respond to family messages promptly and personally. AI can help draft a reply, but the reply should sound like the teacher and address what the parent actually said. If a conversation turns to something sensitive, the teacher should move it to a call with an interpreter. The text does not give separate grade band versions, so this practice is described as the same approach for everyday family conversation.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence for this idea is a health care research finding: research in health care has documented translation errors in real conversations, not just documents (Strechen et al., 2025). The text uses that finding to make the point that two way messaging carries the same accuracy risks as any translation.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that translation tools carry accuracy risks, and the text says two way messaging carries the same accuracy risks as any translation. A reply that feels automated can do more harm than no reply at all, because families notice when they are being handled rather than heard. The translation tool is for everyday conversation, not for serious matters, so if a conversation turns sensitive the teacher should move it to a call with an interpreter. The decisions that stay with a person are to respond promptly and personally, to make the reply sound like the teacher, and to address what the parent actually said. AI can help draft a reply, but it does not replace the teacher's judgment about the message or the choice to move a sensitive conversation to a call.
